A documented price gap

A$12 on the menu. At least A$16 to select it.

A food-delivery listing checked on 15 September 2026 required a paid preparation choice and a paid sauce. Together they added at least A$4 to the displayed A$12 item price1.

Checked 15 September 2026·Australia

Where the extra A$4 appeared

The menu tile showed a chargrilled kebab plate at A$12.00. Inside the item, Choice of Preparation was marked required and its cheapest options added A$3.00. A required sauce added at least A$1.00. At the recorded check, neither group offered a no-cost way to complete the choice1.

Pickup does not remove the item choices

Ub*r e*ts says pickup orders are exempt from delivery and service fees2. Those fees are separate from the required choices inside this item. Choosing pickup could avoid the delivery-related fees, but it did not make the A$12 item selectable without the A$3 preparation and A$1 sauce at this check1.

Why look at this as drip pricing?

The ACCC describes drip pricing as a price advertised early in an online purchase with extra charges added as the customer proceeds. Its price-display guidance says the minimum total should include unavoidable extra costs3.

This one listing shows a clear A$4 gap between the displayed item price and its lowest selectable item price. It does not establish who configured the choices, how common the pattern is, or whether a court would find a legal breach.
